Cloudflare CEO: "Cloudflare Isn't a Neocloud." Maybe That's Why Its Stock Soared as Neoclouds Sank ©@metamorworks from Getty Images via Canva
Key Takeaways

Cloudflare shares jumped 11% after third-quarter revenue rose 39% to $782.5 million. The same week, CoreWeave, Nebius and IREN sank on fears that new rules would limit data center construction.

CEO Matthew Prince called Cloudflare the "first agentic cloud," and its results back up the idea that it can grow with AI agent traffic on a network it already runs.

Quarterly free cash flow has more than doubled since late 2024, and management now expects GAAP profitability in the fourth quarter.

The stock still trades well above its usual forward earnings multiple, so a slowdown in agent traffic would hit it hard.

Cloudflare (NET:NYSE) shares soared 11% today after a blowout third quarter, while CoreWeave (CRWV:NASDAQ) and the rest of the neoclouds kept sinking.

Democrats won control of both chambers of Congress on Tuesday, and investors worried they'd push harder to curb data center construction. CoreWeave fell 10% on Wednesday to a new 52-week low. By Thursday, CoreWeave, Nebius and IREN had each lost more than 10% since the vote. Cloudflare sank 8% right along with them ahead of its report.

Then, on Thursday's third-quarter call, CEO Matthew Prince drew the line himself:

"Cloudflare isn't a neo cloud. We're also not, as some of you have called us, the fourth public cloud. We're something different. We're the first agentic cloud"

Judging by today's jump, investors are buying it.

TIKR tracks 34 analysts on Cloudflare. How many say "Buy"?

See the full breakdown of Buy, Hold, and Sell ratings on Cloudflare, along with Wall Street's revenue and earnings estimates, all in one place. More than 500,000 investors use TIKR to research stocks like this one. See Cloudflare's Analyst Ratings

Agents are moving onto its network

Prince's case starts with how Cloudflare runs code. He said hyperscalers and neoclouds were built around containers. Cloudflare runs on what it calls isolates instead, a lighter way to run many customers' programs on the same machine. He argued that this lets it "scale densely with a level of efficiency no hyperscaler or neo cloud can match."

That efficiency matters because Prince expects agent traffic to dwarf human traffic online, by 1,000 to 1 within five years. He made that call last quarter, and now says he'd "take the under on the timing of that bet."

And the traffic is already showing up. Prince cited third-party data: "between July 1 and today, we added approximately 5% of the entire web to Cloudflare. That's wild." More than 10 million developers were on its platform by October, up from 4.5 million at the end of 2025.

Can it scale profitably? Operating margin hit a record 17.5%. Non-GAAP gross margin did slip quarter over quarter.

Are existing customers expanding? Dollar-based net retention rose to 122%, and large-customer additions were a record.

Does AI demand show up in revenue? Apparently yes. Workers developers doubled to 10M this year. KeyBanc pointed to consumption revenue and "pool of funds" deals. Scotiabank notes traffic growth takes about three quarters to turn into revenue. Scotiabank note (Nov 6, 2026)

Riding the disruption

Genuine disruption often overrides temporary market panic. Cloudflare is no longer just a digital bouncer keeping bad actors off websites; it's positioning itself as the defining network for the next generation of internet traffic.

If autonomous bots are truly poised to outnumber human clicks a thousand to one in the coming years, owning the infrastructure that governs that traffic is a no-brainer. I don't think any other company can match Cloudflare's decades of preparation for this sea change.

Key Takeaways

CrowdStrike rose 2% today after Cloudflare reported 39% revenue growth and raised its full-year outlook.

Cloudflare tied its growth to escalating digital threats, a good sign for security spending.

Palo Alto Networks and Zscaler rose too, ahead of their own reports.

CrowdStrike still trades far above its five-year average multiple, so its Dec. 1 report probably needs another guidance raise.

CrowdStrike (CRWD:NASDAQ) is up 2% today, winning back part of Thursday's 9% drop, and it has another company's quarter to thank.

After Thursday's close, Cloudflare said third-quarter revenue rose 39% to $782.5 million, its fastest growth in nearly four years. It raised its full-year outlook to $2.96 billion, above the $2.87 billion analysts expected. That's good news for Palo Alto Networks (PANW:NASDAQ) and Zscaler (ZS:NASDAQ), too.

Cloudflare puts a number on the threats

Cloudflare co-founder and CEO Matthew Prince tied the growth to the same pressure CrowdStrike sells against: "as digital threats escalate, organizations of every size continue to rely on Cloudflare for protection." He added that Cloudflare has "found an even higher gear for this next phase of growth."

Palo Alto and Zscaler report next

Palo Alto, up 2%, reports first, on Nov. 18. It expects next-generation security ARR of $9.54 billion to $9.56 billion for the quarter ending Oct. 31, up 63%. A beat would say Cloudflare's demand is reaching Palo Alto too.

Zscaler, up 0.1%, competes with Cloudflare in zero-trust security: is that budget growing for both companies, or is Cloudflare taking share? Leaving out its Red Canary acquisition, Zscaler's ARR grew 20% in the year to July 31, and it expects 16.6% to 17.4% growth for the year ahead. Its Dec. 2 report should answer that.

Cloudflare (NET:NYSE) stock is up 11% today after its third-quarter revenue grew at the fastest pace in nearly four years.

That's quite a turnaround from Thursday, when a selloff in cybersecurity stocks pulled down both Cloudflare and Palo Alto Networks (PANW:NASDAQ). Akamai (AKAM:NASDAQ), its oldest rival, reported the same evening, with very different numbers.

Faster, again

Revenue rose 39% to $782.5 million. Analysts expected $739.7 million.

CEO Matthew Prince didn't hold back: "Our engine is firing on all cylinders, and we've found an even higher gear for this next phase of growth."

The guidance backs him up. Cloudflare expects fourth-quarter revenue of $845 million to $846 million, against analysts' $798.2 million.

Going into the report, analysts expected revenue of $2.87 billion this year and $3.70 billion in 2027:

Cloudflare (NET): revenue, actual and consensus estimates, $ billions, fiscal 2023-2028 (TIKR)

If that 2027 figure holds, growth slows to about 25% next year, from about 37% this year. I'd expect it to move up.

Margins are the catch

And the stock was already pricey at 179x forward earnings at Thursday's close, above its 173x average since mid-2023. At today's price, it's even higher.

Akamai's third-quarter revenue rose 6% to $1.12 billion. Its fourth-quarter guidance of $1.145 billion to $1.17 billion fell short of analysts' $1.2 billion. CEO Tom Leighton expects growth to pick up to 17% to 22% in 2027 (adjusted for currency), backed by more than $14 billion of multi-year commitments signed this year for its cloud infrastructure business.

At 13x forward earnings, the market isn't paying for much of that. Can that cloud business keep Cloudflare from pulling further ahead?

Palo Alto is up next
